description: How group size, anonymity and personality affect conformity, and what Asch's line study found.
content_html:
What Is Conformity?

Conformity happens when a person changes their behaviour or belief to match the majority of a group. We often conform without being ordered to — we simply go along with the people around us. Think about a time you stayed quiet when you disagreed with everyone else, or copied how others dressed to fit in. That is conformity in action.

Conformity to majority influence is one of the most studied topics in social psychology. Researchers want to understand why people go along with the crowd even when they suspect the crowd is wrong. Two categories of factors shape conformity: social factors (features of the situation) and dispositional factors (features of the individual).

Social Factors Affecting Conformity

Social factors are things about the social situation that push a person towards or away from conforming. Three key social factors are group size, anonymity and task difficulty.

Group size affects conformity because a larger majority creates more social pressure. The effect grows as the group gets bigger, but eventually levels off — adding more people beyond a certain number does not keep increasing conformity. A group of three or four creates strong pressure; a group of fifteen does not produce much more pressure than a group of seven.

Anonymity reduces conformity. When people can respond privately or without being observed by the group, they feel less pressure to match the majority. They are more willing to give their genuine answer. In contrast, when a person must state their answer publicly in front of the group, conformity rises because they want to avoid looking foolish or different.

Task difficulty also matters. When a task is genuinely hard and the correct answer is unclear, people look to others for guidance. This increases conformity because individuals doubt their own judgement. When the task is easy and the answer is obvious, there is less reason to follow the group — though social pressure may still cause some people to conform.

Dispositional Factors Affecting Conformity

Dispositional factors are characteristics of the individual that influence how likely they are to conform. Two key dispositional factors are personality and expertise.

Personality affects conformity in several ways. People who are high in the need for social approval are more likely to conform because they fear rejection. Those with a strong, independent sense of identity may resist group pressure more easily. Confidence in one’s own judgement is also a personality trait that reduces conformity.

Expertise is the other key dispositional factor. Someone who has specialist knowledge in a topic is less likely to conform to the group’s view because they trust their own informed judgement. For example, a trained mechanic hearing a group of non-experts diagnose a car fault is unlikely to agree simply because they are outnumbered. Their expertise gives them confidence to hold their position.

Key Fact

The three social factors affecting conformity are group size, anonymity and task difficulty. The two dispositional factors are personality and expertise. Larger groups, public responses, harder tasks, approval-seeking personalities and lack of expertise all increase conformity.

Asch’s Study of Conformity

Solomon Asch conducted a classic study to test whether people would conform to a clearly wrong majority. His study is one of the most famous in psychology.

Aim: Asch aimed to investigate whether people would conform to the majority view even when the majority was obviously wrong.

Method: Male participants were placed in a room with several other people (typically seven confederates) who were actually actors working for the researcher. They were shown a card with a standard line and asked to match it to one of three comparison lines of different lengths. The correct answer was always obvious. The confederates had been instructed to give the same wrong answer on 12 out of 18 trials (the critical trials).

Results: Participants gave the wrong answer (matching the majority) on approximately 37% of the critical trials where confederates all gave the wrong answer. Around 75% of participants conformed at least once. When participants responded privately in writing, conformity fell sharply.

Conclusion: Asch concluded that people do conform to majority influence even when the majority is clearly wrong, suggesting that the presence of a unanimous group creates strong social pressure to agree.

Key Fact

In Asch’s conformity study, participants gave wrong answers on around 37% of critical trials, and roughly 75% conformed at least once. When answers were given privately, conformity fell — showing the role of public visibility in creating social pressure.

Evaluating Asch’s Study

Asch’s study has important strengths and weaknesses. A strength is that it was a controlled laboratory experiment, which means the conditions could be carefully controlled and repeated. The use of confederates meant the majority’s behaviour was consistent across trials.

However, there are weaknesses. The sample was limited to male American college students, which means the findings may not apply to women, to other age groups, or to people from different cultures — this reduces generalisability. The artificial lab setting also means the task (comparing line lengths) lacks everyday realism, which reduces ecological validity. Finally, knowing the study involved deception raises ethical concerns about consent, though Asch did debrief participants afterwards.
exam_tip_html: On ‘describe a study’ questions about Asch, you must cover the aim, method, results and conclusion — one sentence each is enough for full marks, but missing any one element will cost you. Don’t just give findings. On 9-mark ‘describe and evaluate’ questions, balance your description of the social and dispositional factors with developed evaluation points (e.g. “low ecological validity because the line task lacks realism” — not just “low ecological validity”).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Conformity is shaped by social factors (group size, anonymity, task difficulty) and dispositional factors (personality, expertise) — larger public groups and harder tasks increase it.
  • Asch’s study found participants conformed on about 37% of critical trials and 75% conformed at least once, even when the correct answer was obvious.
  • Asch’s study is criticised for using an unrepresentative sample and an artificial task, but it clearly demonstrated the power of majority influence in a controlled setting.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes conformity?
A) Obeying a direct order from an authority figure
B) Changing behaviour or belief due to real or imagined group pressure
C) Helping a stranger in an emergency situation
D) Being influenced by an expert in a field
practice_questions.marks: B) Changing behaviour or belief due to real or imagined group pressure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'anonymity' in the context of conformity research.
practice_questions.marks: Anonymity is the condition of not being personally identified or observed by the group [1 mark], which reduces the social pressure to conform because the individual does not fear public judgement or rejection [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe one social factor and one dispositional factor that affect conformity to majority influence.
practice_questions.marks:
Social factor: e.g. group size — as the number of people in the majority increases, the social pressure on the individual to conform also increases [1 mark], though the effect levels off beyond a certain group size [1 mark].
Disposition factor: e.g. expertise — a person with specialist knowledge in the topic is less likely to conform because they trust their own informed judgement rather than the group’s view [1 mark].
[Accept any accurate social factor + dispositional factor with development; 2 marks for the social factor, 1 for the dispositional factor, or 1+2 respectively.]

practice_questions.text: A student is asked to estimate the length of a line in a group activity. She can clearly see the correct answer but the rest of the group all say a different length out loud. Using your knowledge of conformity, explain why she might go along with the group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains two factors clearly linked to the scenario with psychological terminology (e.g. public setting increases social pressure because the student’s response is visible to others; majority group creates pressure to conform to avoid standing out).
Secure: Identifies and explains one factor clearly linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names a relevant factor (e.g. group pressure) but does not link it specifically to the scenario details.
Emerging: Makes a vague reference to fitting in or peer pressure without psychological framing.

Mastering: Accurate aim, method (confederates, line-matching task, 12 critical trials), results (approx. 37% conformity on critical trials, 75% conformed at least once, conformity fell with private responses), and conclusion (people conform to majority even when clearly wrong) — all four elements present and precise.
Secure: Three of the four elements (aim, method, results, conclusion) described accurately with relevant detail.
Developing: Two elements present or one element described in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: A vague account of the study with limited or no specific details about the procedure or findings.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the factors that affect conformity to majority influence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate and detailed description of social factors (group size, anonymity, task difficulty) AND dispositional factors (personality, expertise) with psychological terminology; evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. Asch’s findings support the role of anonymity because conformity fell with private responses; however, the sample lacked diversity, limiting generalisability) with elaboration.
Secure: Description covers most factors with reasonable accuracy; evaluation includes two points with some development.
Developing: Description of two or three factors with some accuracy; evaluation present but limited or repetitive.
Emerging: Brief, underdeveloped description of one or two factors; evaluation is a single sentence without elaboration.

knowledge_checks.q: In Asch's study, approximately what percentage of critical trials did participants give the wrong answer by conforming to the majority?
Which of the following is a dispositional factor affecting conformity?
When a person responds in front of the group rather than privately, _____ decreases and conformity tends to increase.
Asch used _____ who were instructed to give wrong answers to create majority pressure on the real participant.
Match each factor to whether it is social or dispositional:
right: Social factor — the number of people in the majority
Dispositional factor — individual traits such as need for approval
Social factor — difficulty of the task increases doubt and conformity

flashcard_questions.a: A change in behaviour or belief as a result of real or imagined group pressure.

flashcard_questions.q: How does group size affect conformity?
flashcard_questions.a: Larger groups create more social pressure to conform, though the effect levels off beyond a certain size.
Anonymity reduces conformity — people give more genuine answers when not observed by the group.

flashcard_questions.q: How does task difficulty affect conformity?
flashcard_questions.a: Harder tasks increase conformity because individuals doubt their own judgement and look to the group.
Experts are less likely to conform because they trust their own informed judgement over the group.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the aim of Asch's conformity study?
flashcard_questions.a: To investigate whether people would conform to the majority even when it was obviously wrong.

flashcard_questions.q: What role did confederates play in Asch's study?
flashcard_questions.a: They posed as participants and gave the same wrong answer on 12 out of 18 trials.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of critical trials did Asch's participants conform on?
What proportion of Asch's participants conformed at least once?
What happened to conformity in Asch's study when participants responded in writing rather than publicly?
flashcard_questions.a: Conformity fell sharply, showing the role of public visibility.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Asch conclude from his conformity study?
flashcard_questions.a: People conform to majority influence even when the majority is clearly wrong.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of Asch's study related to its sample.
flashcard_questions.a: Only male American college students were used, reducing generalisability to other groups.

glossary_terms.definition: A change in behaviour or belief as a result of real or imagined group pressure.
The number of people in a group, which influences how much pressure is felt to conform.
The condition of not being personally identified, which reduces the social pressure to conform to the group.
Individual personality traits that influence a person's tendency to comply with or resist social pressure.
